paragraphs.heading: The big tides of the month
paragraphs.text: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, driven mainly by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun. The height gap between high and low water over about half a day is called the range. It is not fixed: it grows and shrinks over a two-week cycle. Many shores get two high tides and two low tides each day. A spring tide is the high point of that cycle, when the range is at its largest.

paragraphs.heading: Why spring tides happen
paragraphs.text: About twice a month, near new moon and full moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth form a line. That lined-up position is called a syzygy. The Sun's tidal force then adds to the Moon's instead of working against it. After this alignment, spring tides are sometimes called syzygy tides.

paragraphs.heading: What a spring tide brings
paragraphs.text: During spring tides the high waters climb higher than average and the low waters drop lower. The tides also drive currents that run back and forth, called tidal currents, and these run stronger than usual. The moment such a current stops before turning is called slack water, and at spring tides that pause is shorter than average.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing to do with the season
paragraphs.text: The name has no link to the season of spring. Like the name of that season, it comes from an old sense of jumping, bursting forth or rising. The same idea sits behind the name of a natural spring.

paragraphs.heading: Springs and neaps
paragraphs.text: At first and third quarter moon the Sun and Moon are 90° apart as seen from Earth, and the Sun's force partly cancels the Moon's. The range is then at its smallest, called a neap tide. About seven days pass between a spring tide and a neap. Mean high water springs is the average of the two high tides on spring-tide days, and mean low water springs is the average of the two low tides.
